title: Present active indicative

objectives.can: Give the person and number of a present active indicative and name its subject.
Recognise ten of the commonest verbs.

explanation.summary: A Greek verb form carries its own subject. The ending of λέγει says 'he, she or it says' without any pronoun, and the same stem with -ομεν says 'we say'. This lesson teaches the six present active endings and what the present tense-form usually does.

sections.heading: A verb has a stem and a personal ending
body: A finite verb form is built from a stem that carries the meaning (λεγ- 'say') and an ending that gives the person and number of the subject. Person is first (the speaker: I, we), second (the one spoken to: you) or third (anyone else: he, she, it, they). Number is singular or plural. Three persons in two numbers give six forms.

Because the ending already names the subject, Greek does not need a subject pronoun. Οὐκ ἔχω ἄνδρα in John 4:17 has no word for 'I': the ending -ω is enough. When a pronoun such as ὑμεῖς or ἡμεῖς is added, it usually brings emphasis or contrast, as in John 4:22, where 'you worship' is set against 'we worship'.
A third-person verb may also have its own subject in the nominative, such as ὁ Ἰησοῦς or ἡ γυνή. If it does not, the subject is whoever the context makes clear.

sections.heading: The six endings
body: The present active indicative joins a connecting vowel to the stem, ο before μ and ν, ε elsewhere, and then the personal ending. The first-person singular ends in -ω, which is why verbs are listed by that form: λέγω, 'I say', is the headword for every other form.

Learn the endings as a set (-ω, -εις, -ει, -ομεν, -ετε, -ουσι(ν)). The paradigms below are filled in from verses of the texts, so a gap marked with a dash means that the form does not happen to occur in the texts of the library, not that it does not exist.

sections.heading: Small points of spelling
body: The third-person plural -ουσι(ν) and the verb ἐστί(ν) may end in a movable ν: λέγουσιν or λέγουσι, ἐστίν or ἐστί. The ν is usually added before a vowel or at the end of a sentence, and is often left out before a consonant. It changes nothing in the meaning, so treat the two spellings as one form.

Do not be thrown when a stem changes a little. ἔχω has a rough breathing in the present, and its other tenses use a different stem (ἕξω, ἔσχον). In the present indicative the ending alone tells you the person and number.

sections.heading: What the present does
body: A tense-form in Greek shows how the writer looks at an action, as well as when it takes place. The present usually presents an action as going on or as habitual, and in the indicative it very often refers to the time of speaking: λέγω ὑμῖν, 'I am saying to you'. A good English rendering is sometimes 'I say' and sometimes 'I am saying', and the Greek does not choose between them.

The present can also state a general truth, narrate a past event vividly (the so-called historical present, very common with λέγει in the Gospels), or describe what is about to happen. Do not translate it mechanically; look at the sentence round it.

sections.heading: Reading a sentence
body: Start with the verb. Read its ending to find the person and number, then look for a nominative that agrees with it. If you find one, that is the subject. If you do not, the subject is in the ending. Direct objects stand in the accusative, as in οὐκ ἔχω ἄνδρα.

misunderstandings: Do not look for a separate word 'I' or 'we' before every verb. A bare ἔχω already means 'I have'. If ἐγώ is also there, ask why it is emphasised.
The same ending does not always mean the same person. -ει is third person singular in the present indicative (λέγει) but -εις is second person (λέγεις). Read the last letters.

A form such as λέγων or πιστεύων is not a first-person verb. It is a participle ('saying', 'believing'), which has no person and is taught later. Only the indicative forms in this lesson have the six personal endings.
The present tense-form is not always 'present time' and does not always mean 'is doing'. In narrative λέγει often means 'said'.

deeper.heading: Thematic verbs
body: Grammarians call the verbs of this lesson thematic, because the connecting vowel ο/ε (the thematic vowel) stands between the stem and the ending. A smaller group, the verbs in -μι such as δίδωμι, add the endings straight to the stem. They are met later in the course.

examples.analysis: ἔχω is first person singular, present active indicative, of ἔχω: 'I have'. No pronoun is needed; the ending is the subject. λέγει is third person singular and its subject is ὁ Ἰησοῦς, the nominative later in the clause: here the present narrates a spoken exchange. The last word, ἔχω, is the same form again, in the words Jesus repeats back to her.

(These verbs are contract verbs, the subject of the next lesson, and their endings are changed by contraction.)
